2) City of Navi Mumbai has been planned, designed, and developed by City and Industrial Development of Corporation of Maharashtra Limited (CIDCO), which is a New Town Development Authority and also a Planning Authority under the provisions of Section 113 of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966.

sentences.text: As a part of development of planned city of Navi Mumbai and to provide faster connectivity to Mumbai City, a railway line was planned to be laid.
CIDCO is the land owner in the entire city of Navi Mumbai as the State Government has acquired land and handed it over to CIDCO.

Ordinarily, it is a function of Railways to construct railway stations after General Manger, Central Railway vs The Secretary, Rail Mazdoor Union on 17 October, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/18681859/

sentences.text: However, in the present case, a unique arrangement was made where CIDCO constructed world class railway stations in the city of Navi Mumbai at Vashi, Sanpada, Jui Nagar and Belapur.

As opposed to a usual railway station providing necessary infrastructure for boarding and alighting from trains, CIDCO envisaged construction of railway station complexes including commercial offices, food courts, restaurants, etc for non-railway purposes.
To illustrate, a commercial complex has been built by CIDCO at Vashi Railway Station which houses International Infotech Park.
On similar lines, other railway stations have been constructed by CIDCO at various other points within the city of Navi Mumbai.

3) Since CIDCO was associated with construction of railway stations, it also decided to maintain t h e m , r a t h e r t h a n l e t t i n g R a i l w a y s t o _______________________________________________________________________________ Friday, 17 October 2025 Neeta Sawant WP-576-2007-FC maintain the otherwise swanky railway stations.

Accordingly, an Agreement was executed between CIDCO and Central Railway on 1 August 1998 under which CIDCO took the responsibility of maintaining the railway stations, food court areas, offices of Central Railway Administration etc.
In return, Railways granted advertisement rights to CIDCO to recoup the expenses incurred towards maintenance of the railway stations.
4) According to the Petitioner-Central Railway, CIDCO employed various workers for discharging its obligations under the Agreement dated 1 August 1998 for maintenance of the railway stations.

By letter dated 22 April 1999, Respondent-Union wrote to Regional Labour Commissioner (Central),
raising a dispute relating to 37 workers deployed by CIDCO at various railway stations and sought for regularization of their services into railways on the ground of completion of 240 days of service.
By order dated 24 May 2000, Government of India, Ministry of Labour referred the dispute for adjudication to CGIT.

The Schedule of the reference reads thus :
THE SCHEDULE "Whether the Action of the Management of Central Railway,
Mumbai, by not regularizing the Services of 37 Workmen (Listed in Appendix 'A')
working continuously in the Cleaning, Sweeping, etc., for the last more than four years at the Various Railway Stations of Navi Mumbai is justified?

10) Per contra, Mr. Ramamurthy, the learned counsel appearing for Respondent-Union would oppose the Petition.

He would submit at the very outset that out of total 37 workers on whose behalf Reference was initially made and out of 15 workers on whose behalf the Reference was prosecuted,

13) Rival contentions of the parties now fall for my consideration.

sentences.text: On the other hand, Railways raised a specific plea in its written statement that there was a contract between CIDCO and M/s. Man Power Services.
The CGIT has also recorded a finding in para-9 of the Award that the witness of the Respondent-Union admitted that the workers were engaged by CIDCO and not by Central Railways.

19) Faced with the situation that there are specific admissions by the workers about they being engaged by CIDCO and not by Central Railway, the Tribunal embarked upon the journey of determining the entity for whom the work of maintenance was being executed.
In my view, this is where folly is committed by the Tribunal.
Even if it is assumed that it was the primary responsibility of Railways to maintain its stations, the Tribunal ought to have appreciated the unique facts and circumstances of the present case.
This is not a case where stations are constructed by Railways and are contracted out for maintenance to a contractor.
CIDCO is not a contractor of Railways.
On the other hand, CIDCO is the entity who has constructed the railway stations and possibly owns them.
There appears to be an agreement for execution of lease of railways stations by CIDCO in favour of railways.
Thus, CIDCO is not some sort of a contractor working for railways towards maintenance of stations belonging to railways.
On the other hand, CIDCO has been maintaining its own railway stations which are constructed by it.

Therefore, the role of CIDCO cannot be confused with that of a c o n t r a c t o r p e r f o r m i n g t h e w o r k o f m a i n t a i n i n g r a i l w a y s t a t i o n s o n b e h a l f _______________________________________________________________________________ Friday, 17 October 2025 Neeta Sawant WP-576-2007-FC of Railways.
Therefore, the entire approach of CGIT while deciding the Reference appears to be faulty.
20) The findings recorded by the Tribunal that the property on which the work is performed is property of Central Railway also appears to be not in tune with the factual position.

There is nothing on record to indicate that the ownership or leasehold rights in respect of railway stations are transferred by CIDCO to Central Railway and in absence of such material, CGIT could not have recorded a finding that the property belongs to Central Railway.
Mere issuance of authority by Station Managers to enter railway stations would not make the concerned workers, employees of Railways in any manner.

The Tribunal has also erred in holding that the arrangement of execution of Agreement is for the convenience of Central Railway and for its benefit and that the workers were actually working for Central Railway.

Another grossly erroneous finding recorded by the CGIT is found to be in para-12 of the Award wherein it has been held as under :

but there is sub-contract also implemented by the 1st Party.
When there was ban on Contract Labour regarding perennial nature of work, question arises how this type of development took place and who permitted them to do it? ...

21) The CGIT has thus erroneously assumed that there was a contract/sub-contract between Central Railways and M/s. Man Power Services.

It further erred in embarking upon an enquiry about ban under the provisions of CLRA Act ignoring the position that the alleged principal worker in the present case is CIDCO who has contracted out the work to M/s. Man Power Services.
In any case, the Notification dated 9 December 1976 issued under the provisions of Section 10(1) of the CLRA Act has been set aside by the Constitution Bench in Steel Authority of India Ltd (supra).

There is neither any Notification prohibiting engagement of contract workers nor any finding is recorded by CGIT that alleged sub-contract between Railways and M/s Man Power Services is sham or bogus.

Therefore, the ratio of the judgment in Kirloskar Brothers (supra) and International Airport Authority of India (supra)
would squarely apply to the present case.

In para-12 to 14 of the judgment in Kirloskar Brothers, it is held as under :
12.

sentences.text: It is further observed that where there is no notification under Section 10 of the CLRA Act and where it is not proved in the industrial adjudication that the contract was a sham/nominal and camouflage, then the question of directing the principal employer to absorb or regularise the services of the contract labour does not arise.
It has further been observed in paras 38 and 39 as under: ( International Airport Authority of India case, SCC p. 388) "38.

The tests that are applied to find out whether a person is an employee or an independent contractor may not automatically apply in finding out whether the contract labour agreement is a sham, nominal and is a mere camouflage.

For example, if the contract is for supply of labour, necessarily,
the labour supplied by the contractor will work under the directions, supervision and control of the principal employer but that would not make the worker a direct employee of the principal employer, if the salary is paid by a contractor, if the right to regulate the employment is with the contractor, and the ultimate supervision and control lies with the contractor.
39. The principal employer only controls and directs the work to be done by a contract labour, when such labour is assigned/allotted/sent to him.
But it is the contractor as employer, who chooses whether the worker is to be assigned/allotted to the principal employer or used otherwise.

In short, worker being the employee of the contractor, the ultimate supervision and control lies with the contractor as he decides where the employee will work and how long he will work and subject to what conditions.

Only when the contractor assigns/sends the worker to work under the p r i n c i p a l  
e m p l o y e r ,

The primary control is with the contractor."

22) There is no finding recorded by CGIT in the entire Award that either contract between Central Railway and CIDCO or the alleged sub-contract between Railways and M/s. Man Power Services is sham or bogus.
On the other hand, the CGIT has treated the contract between CIDCO and Central Railway to be genuine one in para-11 of the Award.
In absence of a finding that a contract or sub-contract is sham or bogus, it was not permissible for CGIT to treat the workers as direct workers of Railways.

For granting relief of regularisation in favour of the workers, the Tribunal had an uphill task of holding first that the contract between CIDCO and Central Railways is sham and bogus and thereafter the further contract between CIDCO and M/s.
Man Power Services is also sham and bogus.
It is only after both the contracts are treated as sham and bogus, it could have been possible to hold the concerned workers as direct railway employees.
The Tribunal has however not undertaken the exercise of determining whether either or both the contracts are sham or bogus.

In Balwant Rai Saluja (supra) the Apex Court has laid down six tests in para- 65 of the judgment as under :

sentences.text: Even otherwise, none of the six tests get satisfied in the present case for the purpose of establishing direct employer-employee relationship between the Railways and the workers.
The workers are not appointed by the Central Railway and therefore, the first test fails.
The workers have never been paid salary/wages by Central Railway and accordingly, second test also fails.

Central Railway does not have authority to dismiss the workers or to take disciplinary action against them and nothing is brought on record to indicate that any worker is dismissed by Central Railway or any disciplinary proceedings are initiated by the Railways.
Therefore, the third and fourth tests also fail.
With regard to the fifth test of continuity of service, only 6 workers claim continuance in service out of 37 workers initially involved in the Reference.

The last test of control and supervision also fails as no material is brought on record to indicate that the decisions relating to leave, service conditions,
ACRs, deployment etc. are ever taken by Central Railway.
Thus, five out of the six tests prescribed in Balwant Rai Saluja (supra) are admittedly not fulfilled in the present case.

Therefore, even if the Tribunal was to conduct an enquiry into the employer- employee relationship between Railways and workers, such enquiry would not have yielded any positive outcome in favour of the workers.
In my view therefore, the CGIT has erred in allowing the Reference and directing regularization of workers on establishment of Railways.
Railways are an instrumentality of State.
Appointments in Railways need to be done in accordance with Recruitment Rules, against sanctioned posts and after following due process of selection.
This is the mandate of the provisions of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India.
The workers engaged by a contractor of CIDCO cannot be directed to be absorbed in railway service when there is no semblance of employer-employee relationship between the duo.
Such absorption would be contrary to the mandate of the Constitution Bench judgment in Umadevi (supra).

sentences.text: Coming to the last submission of Mr. Ramamurthy, which is more equitable in nature, he urges the Court to uphold the Tribunal's order as only six workers will be benefited by the Award, who currently continue to work on maintenance work of railway stations.
This Court therefore raised a query as to who is paying them wages as of now.

Ms. Thakur has clarified the position by placing on record copy of letter dated 9 October 2025 by Senior DOM (G) which reads thus :
 No. BB/T/240/CLO/01 Date: 09-10-2025  Law Officer
Mumbai Division Sub: Clarification regarding deployment of manpower and payment of wages at stations maintained by CIDCO.

With reference to the above, it is clarified that:
1. This office does not deploy any manpower for cleanliness or related activities at the stations maintained by CIDCO.
2. The wages of labourers working at the stations under CIDCO's maintenance are not paid by this office.

3. The station cleanliness contract managed by this office covers the Harbour Line section from Dockyard Road to Mankhurd stations only, and contractual staff are deployed exclusively within this section for execution of cleanliness work.
This is for your kind information and necessary record please.
B. Arun Kumar Sr. DOM(G)-BB 26)

Thus, on the Harbour line of Central Railway, there is still a clear demarcation where the Railways manage cleanliness of stations only upto Mankhurd station and all stations in Navi Mumbai are maintained by CIDCO.
Thus, even today, the wages of the workers are apparently paid by CIDCO either by itself or through contractors.
The wages are not paid by Central Railway in any manner.
Mere grant of advertisement rights to CIDCO by Railways cannot be a reason enough to presume that the wages are paid to the workers by the Railways in an indirect manner.

While the suggestion for absorption of services of only six workers may appear attractive in the first blush, the same would have serious repercussions for Railways as the same would invite spate of litigations in r e s p e c t o f o t h e r w o r k e r s e n g a g e d i n m a i n t e n a n c e w o r k o f _______________________________________________________________________________ General Manger, Central Railway vs The Secretary, Rail Mazdoor Union

From letter dated 8 August 2018, it appears that CIDCO is still maintaining the railway stations and in the process, it may have contracted out manpower related services to several contractors.
If the claim of six workers for absorption in railway services is accepted purely on equitable or sympathetic grounds, hundreds of other workers would stake similar claims.
Therefore, granting relief of absorption by applying the consideration of small number of workers (six) would not be a correct approach.
It is claimed that the said six workers are in continuous services since 1992-95.
If that is the case, it would be open for them to claim absorption in service with CIDCO.
Granting them absorption in Railways is something which is not possible considering the unique facts and circumstances of the present case.

It further erred in embarking upon an enquiry about ban under the provisions of CLRA Act ignoring the position that the alleged principal worker in the present case is CIDCO who has contracted out the work to M/s. Man Power Services.
In any case, the Notification dated 9 December 1976 issued under the provisions of Section 10(1) of the CLRA Act has been set aside by the Constitution Bench in Steel Authority of India Ltd (supra).
There is neither any Notification prohibiting engagement of contract workers nor any finding is recorded by CGIT that alleged sub-contract between Railways and M/s Man Power Services is sham or bogus.
In the present case, neither any notification under Section 10(1) of CLRA Act has been issued prohibiting the contract labour, nor there are allegations and/or even findings that the contract is sham and bogus and/or camouflage.
